passage: The association between cadence and biomechanical efficiency across varying locomotor speeds has been examined in the literature, with findings suggesting complex relationships between self-selected stepping frequency and lower extremity loading patterns. The magnitude of cadence-related changes in kinetic and kinematic variables has varied considerably across populations and imposed conditions.

Ground contact time and its relationship to overall gait cycle characteristics have been examined across different running speeds and surface conditions. Evidence regarding the mechanistic associations between contact phase duration and force production has demonstrated variable patterns, with inconsistent findings regarding the contribution of stance time to dynamic stability.

The examination of flight phase duration and its association with propulsive mechanics has revealed varied relationships across different locomotor demands. Findings have demonstrated that aerial time fluctuates with changes in cadence and speed, though the magnitude of these associations has shown inconsistent patterns in the literature.

Associations between the proportion of the gait cycle spent in contact with the ground and overall biomechanical stability have been examined, with evidence suggesting moderate correlations to locomotor efficiency. The relationship between duty factor and lower extremity joint loading has varied across populations and movement conditions.

Stride length and its relationship to metabolic cost and lower extremity joint mechanics have been examined across a range of self-selected and imposed conditions. Findings regarding the magnitude of stride length effects on knee and ankle loading have demonstrated variable associations, with evidence for both trivial and moderate correlations depending on population characteristics.

The association between vertical centre of mass displacement and metabolic expenditure during running has been examined, with evidence suggesting moderate correlations to locomotor economy. Findings have varied regarding the mechanistic contribution of vertical excursion to propulsive force generation and overall movement efficiency.

Relationships between normalised vertical oscillation and spatiotemporal gait characteristics have been examined across diverse running populations. Evidence regarding the association between this ratio and running economy has demonstrated inconsistent findings, with variable correlations observed across different cadence and speed conditions.

The association between foot landing position relative to the body's centre of mass and braking force magnitude has been examined in the running mechanics literature. Findings regarding the relationship between overstriding and lower extremity impact loading have demonstrated variable patterns, with evidence suggesting both trivial and moderate mechanistic contributions depending on running speed and surface characteristics.

Foot strike pattern and its association with instantaneous ground reaction forces have been examined across different running speeds and populations. Findings regarding the relationship between foot contact angle and sagittal plane joint loading have varied considerably, with evidence for inconsistent mechanistic pathways to injury risk.

The association between knee flexion angle at initial contact and shock attenuation mechanisms has been examined in the biomechanics literature. Findings have demonstrated varied relationships between sagittal knee kinematics at footstrike and proximal and distal joint loading patterns, with evidence suggesting moderate to inconsistent correlations across different running speeds and footwear conditions.

Relationships between forward trunk inclination and lower extremity joint loading have been examined across a range of running conditions and populations. Findings regarding the magnitude of trunk flexion effects on sagittal plane knee and hip mechanics have demonstrated variable associations, with evidence suggesting both trivial and moderate mechanistic pathways to altered force distribution patterns.
